evidence_excerpt: A well-structured and managed system emphasizing safety would have flagged the rising doubts about the Solid Rocket Booster joint seal.
source_ref: Rogers Commission Report, Vol. I, Chapter V, finding 1
justification: L2 validity conditions met: (C1) the teleconference minutes and sworn testimony show Thiokol management exited the caucus with a unanimous launch-recommend output after exclusion of dissenting engineers; (C2) a procedural alternative of weighing engineering input on merits does not predict the observed narrowing of dissent to the caucus room; (C3) survives counter that experienced managers may legitimately override engineering caution, because override requires substantive rebuttal of the data which the record does not contain.

evidence_excerpt: Mr. Jerald Mason turned to Mr. Robert Lund and said, 'Take off your engineering hat and put on your management hat.'
source_ref: Rogers Commission Report, Vol. I, Chapter V
justification: L1 conditions: (C1) a quoted direct instruction from senior management to a subordinate to reframe a technical judgment as a managerial one; (C2) the procedural explanation that management was simply broadening criteria does not require subordinating the engineering assessment; (C3) survives counter that 'management hat' meant weighing broader considerations, because no additional considerations appear in the record before the reversal.

mode_name: Optimism bias / normalization of prior success
evidence_excerpt: Erosion was a clue that something was wrong. Erosion was not something from which safety could be inferred.
source_ref: Rogers Commission Vol. II, Appendix F (Feynman)
justification: L1 conditions: (C1) the record shows NASA managers interpreted observed but partial O-ring erosion on prior flights as validating a safety margin, not as an anomaly; (C2) the operative decision-rule treated non-failure as positive evidence of safety, which is a canonical optimism-bias signature; (C3) survives counter that treating flight history as empirical data is standard engineering, because engineering standard practice treats unexpected erosion as a warning, not a margin.

evidence_excerpt: Meeting flight schedules and cutting costs were given a higher priority than flight safety.
source_ref: Investigation of the Challenger Accident, House Report 99-1016 (1986), pp. 4-6
justification: L4g conditions: (C1) the House Committee and the Rogers Commission both document that Thiokol management's recommendation-reversal and Marshall's acceptance of it were conditioned on schedule and cost considerations; (C2) the engineering safety concern constitutes a technical externality to the contracting/schedule decision frame; (C3) the record shows the engineering data was dismissed without substantive engagement (no rebuttal of the temperature correlation was entered into the decision record before the recommendation flip).

evidence_excerpt: The Commission is troubled by what appears to be a propensity of management at Marshall to contain potentially serious problems and to attempt to resolve them internally rather than communicate them forward.
source_ref: Rogers Commission Report, Vol. I, Chapter V
justification: L5f conditions: (C1) the decision-authority boundary (Marshall Level II) and the information-scope boundary (engineering O-ring history held at Thiokol plus select Marshall engineers) did not align, so the jurisdiction holding launch authority did not coincide with the jurisdiction holding the risk-relevant information; (C2) this is a structural, not individual, failure — the org chart and the flight-readiness process both permitted Level II to terminate escalation; (C3) survives counter that this is just L2 groupthink, because the pattern persisted across multiple tenure cycles at Marshall and is described in the Rogers finding as a 'propensity' rather than an episode.
